elasticity_benchmarks.notes: A 5% price rise typically cuts unit sales by 8-12%. Shoppers compare prices online before buying, and festive sales (October-November) bring about 35% of yearly volume.

Branded sneakers with similar designs are easy to compare, so a 5% price rise cuts units by 7-10%. Store-brand footwear is less compared (Medium elasticity). The festive season sells about 30% of yearly volume.
Style and fit matter more than price for fashion items. Basics such as plain T-shirts and jeans behave like High elasticity because they are easy to compare.
Price signals exclusivity. Demand is driven by brand, scarcity and gifting seasons, and discounts can damage how customers see the brand.
Staples are necessities, so total demand barely moves with price, but shoppers notice the prices of key value items (rice, oil, milk, atta) and switch stores over them.
Cookware and appliances are compared online, but brand trust and warranty let well-known brands sell slightly above unbranded alternatives.

historical_margins.notes: Smartphones 8-12%, laptops and TVs 10-15%, audio 18-25%, accessories 35-55%. Thin margins on big items are made up by accessories sold with them.
Branded sneakers priced above a 40% margin sold less than 60% of stock at full price.
End-of-season markdowns of 20-35% bring the realised margin down to about 42%.
Full-price sell-through matters more than margin; discounts above 10% have not paid off.
Products priced more than 10% above competitors needed clearance markdowns.

competitor_trends.trend: Online marketplaces sell smartphones, laptops and TVs 3-6% below store prices and add 5-10% bank-card offers in festive sales. Competitors match a price cut within 1-2 days, so a cut wins extra volume only briefly.

Entry-level branded lifestyle sneakers cluster in the ₹2,199-₹2,999 band, and few sell above ₹3,000 without a performance feature. Online marketplaces list the same models 5-10% lower during sale events.
Fast-fashion competitors start end-of-season sales (30-50% off) in late June and late December. Basics are priced to the rupee against competitors; fashion pieces are not directly comparable.

Brands set recommended prices and authorised competitors rarely discount. Grey-market online sellers list 10-20% below, but most luxury shoppers buy from authorised stores for authenticity and warranty.
Competitors price key value items (rice, oil, milk, atta) 1-3% below the printed price to bring shoppers in. Quick-commerce apps charge 2-5% more but win on speed.
Cookware prices are compared online. Competitors run bundle offers (buy 2, get 10% off) more often than straight price cuts.

pricing_guidelines.title: High elasticity: small price changes
pricing_guidelines.rule: Change prices in small steps of no more than 3-5% at a time, and stay within 3% of the main competitor. Prefer pricing slightly below the competitor when the margin allows.
pricing_guidelines.rationale: Price-sensitive shoppers switch quickly after a large increase, and competitors match large cuts within days.

pricing_guidelines.title: Medium elasticity: price near the competitor
pricing_guidelines.rule: Price within 5% of the competitor. Go above it only when brand, quality or service clearly sets the product apart.
pricing_guidelines.rationale: Shoppers compare, but they will pay a little more for a product they prefer.

pricing_guidelines.title: Low elasticity: protect price and brand
pricing_guidelines.rule: Price at or up to 10% above the competitor when the brand justifies it, and avoid discounts above 10%.
pricing_guidelines.rationale: Volume barely changes with price, so discounts give away margin, and frequent sales teach customers to wait.

pricing_guidelines.title: Never price below the margin floor
pricing_guidelines.rule: The minimum price is cost / (1 - target margin). If the market price is below this floor, keep the floor price and compete on value (bundles, service), or escalate to the category manager.
pricing_guidelines.rationale: A price below the floor misses the target margin on every unit sold.

pricing_guidelines.title: Psychological price points
pricing_guidelines.rule: End mass-market prices in 99 or 49 (for example ₹2,499 or ₹2,599). Use round prices (for example ₹35,000) for luxury goods.
pricing_guidelines.rationale: Prices ending in 99 read as good value, but on luxury goods they look like a discount.

pricing_guidelines.title: Passing on cost increases
pricing_guidelines.rule: Pass on cost increases in steps of no more than 5%. In high elasticity categories, absorb part of the increase for a season.
pricing_guidelines.rationale: A single large increase triggers the sharpest drop in volume.

pricing_guidelines.title: Festive and sale periods
pricing_guidelines.rule: Use temporary festive discounts of 5-10% rather than permanent price cuts, and plan them 4-6 weeks ahead.
pricing_guidelines.rationale: A temporary discount wins seasonal volume without resetting the regular price.

pricing_guidelines.title: Categories with no history
pricing_guidelines.rule: If a category has no benchmarks or past decisions, start at the floor price for the target margin, stay within 5% of the competitor, and review after 4 weeks of sales.
pricing_guidelines.rationale: Without evidence, a cautious price limits the risk of a wrong guess.
